parts.title: The Tuatara of New Zealand
parts.article:
The Tuatara of New Zealand
 
(A) Tuatara are lizard-like reptiles found only in New Zealand. They are representative of ancient life forms. Tuatara are the sole surviving members of an ancient lineage of reptiles called Sphenodontia, which is over 250 million years old. Because tuatara still resemble fossils of reptiles that lived during the age of dinosaurs, they are often called “living fossils”. Now only two species survive in New Zealand. One is the Brothers Island tuatara which, until recent re-introductions to sanctuaries (safe places for wildlife), survived only on North Brother Island. The other species is the common tuatara, which inhabits many other offshore islands. Although the two species appear similar, they have genetic differences. Tuatara bones have been found in many parts of New Zealand; where dated, they are usually a few hundred to 5,000 years old. It is not known whether these bones belong to the two living species or to others that are now extinct.
 
(B) Many anatomical features distinguish tuatara from other living reptiles—for example, they have a distinctive pattern of openings in the skull, a unique type of haemoglobin in the blood, and males have no external reproductive organ. Adults range from 30 to 75 centimetres in length and weigh between 250 and 1,200 grams. Males are larger than females and have more developed spines in the crest along the neck, back and tail.
 
(C) The male tuatara courts the female by approaching her with a proud walk. Tuatara mate in late summer, and the female usually lays 6–10 eggs the following spring in a shallow ground-level nest. She may guard the nest for a few nights, then return to her underground burrow. The eggs incubate for about a year, so hatchlings emerge just as new eggs are being laid the next season. Evidence indicates that the sex of hatchlings is determined by both genetic and environmental factors: warmer eggs are more likely to produce males, while cooler eggs tend to produce females. The hatchlings receive no parental care and must find their own food.
 
(D) Tuatara live a long time, reaching reproductive maturity at about 15 years and breeding for many decades. Their maximum lifespan is uncertain, but many individuals have lived to 80 years while still looking vigorous and healthy. Tuatara live in underground burrows and are more active at night, though they bask in the sun by day. Both sexes are territorial; males aggressively defend their range by posturing and, if necessary, fighting. Their teeth are their chief weapons, and a bite can cause serious injury. Tuatara are carnivorous, feeding on invertebrates, lizards and the baby seabirds with which they often share burrows.
 
(E) Tuatara were once widespread and abundant on the New Zealand mainland, but when Polynesian settlers arrived (about 1250–1300 AD) they brought Pacific rats, which killed tuatara. By the time of European settlement in the 1840s, tuatara were almost extinct on the mainland. Some islands provided temporary refuges, but these too were eventually invaded by rats and other mammalian predators.
 
(F) Gradually tuatara became confined to 32 near-shore islands. Many of these islands were tiny, some only one hectare in size. A few, such as the Poor Knights Islands off the northeastern coast of New Zealand and some islands in Cook Strait, still support the common tuatara. The Brothers Island tuatara survived only on North Brother Island, but new populations have been created on Titi Island in the Marlborough Sounds and on Somes Island in Wellington Harbour.
 
(G) Tuatara can live in remarkably dense populations. Most tuatara islands support 50–100 individuals per hectare, so an island of just 10 hectares may hold hundreds. Larger islands rich in seabirds and invertebrates—key tuatara prey—may support even greater densities. The largest population is on Stephens Island, where numbers reach up to 2,500 per hectare in some areas, with a total of at least 30,000 individuals. Overall, the tuatara population across all islands is estimated at 50,000–100,000.
 
(H) Legal protection was granted to tuatara and their islands in 1895, yet the reptiles continued to decline. Since then, active conservation management has reversed the trend, and new populations have been established on predator-free islands. In the mid-1980s the New Zealand Wildlife Service (now the Department of Conservation) developed methods to eradicate rats from islands. Rats have since been removed from almost all tuatara islands, making these habitats safe for many threatened native species. Conservationists have also collected eggs for incubation, bred tuatara in captivity, and relocated them to rat-free islands off the Northland coast and to Stephens Island in Cook Strait—areas never invaded by rats and largely free of other mammalian predators. Two additional predator-free islands now host tuatara, raising the total to 37. Many more introductions are planned for islands and mainland reserves cleared of predators.

Questions 1–6
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 1–6 on your answer sheet, write:

Q1 The two living species of tuatara look alike.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q2 Many tuatara bones that have been discovered are millions of years old.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q3 The tails of male tuatara are a different colour from those of female tuatara.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q4 The female tuatara lays her eggs in a burrow.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q5 There are more female hatchlings than male hatchlings.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q6 Once they have hatched, young tuatara have to look after themselves.

  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

reference:
Q1

干扰 你可能看到后面半句写着“genetic differences”（基因差异）就想选FALSE，但题目问的是长相（look）而不是基因。

句子 [第2段] Although the two species appear similar, they have genetic differences.

解析 原文明确指出这两个现存物种“appear similar”（看起来相似），直接对应题目中的“look alike”。

Q2

解析 原文说被发现的骨头通常只有几百到5000年的历史，这与题目声称的“millions of years”（数百万年）完全矛盾。

干扰 你可能会和第一段提到的“over 250 million years old”那个物种起源时间混淆，但题目问的是“挖出来的骨头（bones）”的年份。

句子 [第3段] Tuatara bones have been found in many parts of New Zealand; where dated, they are usually a few hundred to 5,000 years old.

Q3

解析 原文对比雄性和雌性时，只提到了体型大小（larger）和尾部棘刺的发达程度（more developed spines），根本没提过“colour”（颜色）。

干扰 不要因为原文确实对比了雌雄的尾巴（tail），就自行脑补它们颜色也不一样，没有提及就是NOT GIVEN。

句子 [第4段] Males are larger than females and have more developed spines in the crest along the neck, back and tail.

Q4

干扰 你可能看到了后面的“return to her underground burrow”就匆忙选对，但她只是回洞穴，下蛋是在外面的地表巢穴里完成的。

解析 原文说雌性把蛋产在地面的浅巢（ground-level nest）里，而不是题目所说的地下洞穴（burrow）里。

句子 [第5段] Tuatara mate in late summer, and the female usually lays 6-10 eggs the following spring in a shallow ground-level nest. She may guard the nest for a few nights, then return to her underground burrow.

Q5

解析 原文只介绍了温度会影响孵化出雌雄的概率（暖生雄，冷生雌），但并没有给出整体上雌性多还是雄性多的“数量对比”结果。

干扰 看到对比不要激动，原文是机制对比，题目是结果（数量）对比，两者不能划等号。

句子 [第5段] Evidence indicates that the sex of hatchlings is determined by both genetic and environmental factors: warmer eggs are more likely to produce males, while cooler eggs tend to produce females.

Q6

解析 原文说刚孵化的小蜥蜴得不到父母的照顾且必须自己找食物，这完美同义替换了题目中的“look after themselves”（照顾自己）。

干扰 只要认识“no parental care”（没有父母照顾）和“find their own food”（自己找吃的），这道题的同义替换是非常直接的。

句子 [第5段] The hatchlings receive no parental care and must find their own food.

Q7

句子 [第6段] Their maximum lifespan is uncertain, but many individuals have lived to 80 years while still looking vigorous and healthy.

干扰 紧跟着表示年龄的数字提取即可，不要填错成前面的成熟年龄“15”。

解析 题目问许多个体至少能活到多少岁，原文直接给出了数字“80 years”。

Q8

解析 题目问它们用什么攻击其他生物，原文说“Their teeth are their chief weapons”（牙齿是主要武器），所以填teeth。

干扰 你需要把题目中的“attack”（攻击）和原文的“weapons / bite”（武器/咬）对应起来，锁定它们所指的身体部位。

句子 [第6段] Both sexes are territorial; males aggressively defend their range by posturing and, if necessary, fighting. Their teeth are their chief weapons, and a bite can cause serious injury.

Q9

解析 题目问它们吃什么同居在洞穴里的幼小动物（young），原文对应的是“baby seabirds”（幼年海鸟）。

干扰 题目中的“young”对应原文的“baby”，不要填成了并列的其他食物（如invertebrates或lizards），因为它们不符合“young”这个修饰词。

句子 [第6段] Tuatara are carnivorous, feeding on invertebrates, lizards and the baby seabirds with which they often share burrows.

Q10

句子 [第7段] Tuatara were once widespread and abundant on the New Zealand mainland, but when Polynesian settlers arrived (about 1250-1300 AD) they brought Pacific rats, which killed tuatara.

解析 题目问老鼠是由什么人带来的，原文说是“Polynesian settlers”（波利尼西亚定居者）带来的，所以填Polynesian。

干扰 题目空后面有一个“people”（人），所以你需要填一个修饰人的词，原文的“settlers”就是people的同义替换，修饰它的就是Polynesian。

Q11

解析 题目问到了1840年代，几乎在什么地方找不到它们了，原文说在“mainland”（大陆）上近乎绝迹（almost extinct）。

干扰 题目中的“hardly any... were found”完美替换了原文的“almost extinct”（几乎绝迹），定位后直接照抄地点名词即可。

句子 [第7段] By the time of European settlement in the 1840s, tuatara were almost extinct on the mainland.

Q12

解析 题目问这些特定岛屿上现在栖息着哪种tuatara，原文明确给出了物种名称“the common tuatara”。

干扰 原文里提到了两个品种（Brothers Island和common），一定要通过题目里给出的地点（north-eastern coast / Cook Strait）来精准锁定是“common”。

句子 [第8段] A few, such as the Poor Knights Islands off the north-eastern coast of New Zealand and some islands in Cook Strait, still support the common tuatara.

Q13

解析 题目问Stephens岛上每公顷的密度高达多少，原文直接给出数字“2,500 per hectare”。

干扰 这题非常直白，只要通过大写专有名词“Stephens Island”定位，再找到“per hectare”前面的数字即可，不会填错。

句子 [第9段] The largest population is on Stephens Island, where numbers reach up to 2,500 per hectare in some areas...
